strengths: Addresses a relevant practical problem: integrating multiple MLLMs without additional training, with genuine benefits for extensibility and modularity
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 10+ diverse benchmarks spanning general understanding, vision, temporal reasoning, and specialized domains
Thoughtful system design with three well-motivated components addressing distinct challenges (task routing, memory management, latency optimization)
Strong empirical results on multiple benchmarks (88.54% on MMBench-EN, 70.04% on MMMU, notable improvements on video understanding)
Clear presentation with effective figures illustrating the framework and concrete workflow examples
Practical system that demonstrates feasibility of achieving multimodal capabilities through intelligent orchestration rather than end-to-end training
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Unfair experimental comparisons - the system uses multiple large models (7+ expert models) as executors while comparing against single models (GPT-4o, VITA). The paper acknowledges 60% of calls to 32B model but does not properly address this fundamental unfairness. Fair comparisons require joint training baselines or equal computational budget comparisons.

Insufficient computational cost analysis - claims 10.3% latency reduction but only measures TTS time (0.204→0.183s), not total system latency, FLOPs, or memory requirements. Efficiency claims are not substantiated given the use of multiple large models running in sequence with orchestration overhead.

No ablation studies provided - impossible to assess individual component contributions (controller, memory, parallel TTS). Cannot determine whether improvements come from routing, memory pooling, or task-specific expert selection. The 7.8% video improvement is attributed broadly without mechanistic analysis.

Limited technical novelty - controller routing uses straightforward prompt engineering with special tokens (not novel), memory system uses standard JSON storage (used in existing agents), parallel batch TTS is engineering optimization. Contribution is primarily system-level integration rather than methodological advances.

Reproducibility concerns - many baseline results 'referenced from official papers' rather than reproduced under identical conditions; critical implementation details under-specified (control token definition, token generation mechanism, runtime prompt construction, fallback behaviors); no code release mentioned

Misleading 'training-free' framing - all components (controller LLM and expert models) are pre-trained; only composition lacks training. More accurately 'composition without additional training,' not 'training-free,' overselling the novelty

Missing failure mode analysis - no investigation of when orchestration fails, error rates in control token generation, or performance degradation under model selection errors. Sensitivity to incorrect routing decisions not addressed.

Vague critical design specifications - memory compression strategy left unspecified (rule-based vs auxiliary LLM), runtime prompt construction inadequately detailed, semantic classification for modality selection lacks implementation details, TTS segmentation rules are basic heuristics without comparison to alternatives

Insufficient ablation and sensitivity analysis - no study showing impact of removing orchestration reasoning vs simple routing, no prompt sensitivity analysis, no investigation of controller LLM size effects, no comparison of different expert model combinations

Limited analysis of complex multimodal reasoning - example workflow (garden flowers) is simple; no analysis of challenging multi-step tasks requiring true cross-modal understanding; specialized task performance highly variable (MathVision 39.11% vs CC-OCR 79.11%) without explanation

strengths: Clear motivation for combining heterogeneous multimodal models without retraining
Comprehensive evaluation across diverse benchmarks (MMBench, MMStar, MMMU, specialized tasks)
Well-organized presentation with generally clear writing and informative figures
Practical engineering contributions: modular framework design and parallel TTS optimization (10.3% latency reduction)
Extensible architecture using special tokens for easy integration of new modalities
weaknesses: Unfair experimental comparisons: achieves 88.54% vs VITA's 71.80% on MMBench, but uses a substantially larger 32B executor model (60% of calls) while VITA uses smaller base models. This confounds orchestration contribution with model size differences, invalidating the claimed performance improvements.

Insufficient technical novelty: LLM-based task routing via prompting is standard in agent systems (AutoGen, TaskWeaver, LangChain). Cross-modal memory is basic JSON serialization. Parallel TTS synthesis is a standard optimization. The core components are well-established techniques, not research contributions.

Missing critical ablation studies: No evaluation of individual component contributions (memory module, special tokens, memory compression). Impossible to determine what actually drives performance gains.

Incomplete multimodal evaluation: Most benchmarks are vision-only or vision-centric. Limited true multimodal fusion evaluation requiring simultaneous vision+audio+text integration. No user studies validating claimed 'natural interaction' capabilities. No failure mode analysis.

Computational cost not properly analyzed: Total system cost (multiple models + controller routing overhead) compared to single end-to-end models not thoroughly evaluated. The claimed 10.3% TTS improvement is marginal relative to overall latency. No resource usage comparison with training-based approaches.

Algorithm and technical details lack rigor: Modality selection δ_modality is trivial token-matching. Memory compression function h_compress is vaguely described as either 'rule-based' or 'auxiliary LLM' with no evaluation. Integration function I(·) never formally defined. No analysis of routing reliability or failure rates.

Overclaimed novelty and misleading framing: Abstract claims '7.8% improvement over jointly-trained approaches' without clarifying this is due to using larger executor models. Terms like 'training-free' and 'intelligent orchestration' overstate what is essentially prompt engineering.

Limited research contribution: While demonstrating orchestration feasibility is useful engineering, it does not constitute sufficient novelty for ICML. The work applies existing agent patterns to multimodal setting without algorithmic innovation or rigorous theoretical analysis.
Reproducibility concerns: Code availability not mentioned. Some results 'referenced from official papers' rather than reproduced. Exact baseline configurations sometimes unclear.

Problem formulation issues: Claims to solve 'modal alignment' but merely defers to pre-trained models without achieving actual representation-level alignment. 'Extensibility' advantages over fine-tuning are overstated.

strengths: Strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks: 88.54% on MMBench-EN (vs 83.10% GPT-4o), 70.04% on MMMU (vs 59.20%), and 7.8% improvement on video tasks demonstrate competitive performance.
Well-motivated practical problem with clear practical value: avoiding expensive training/retraining cycles and enabling rapid modality integration.
Clear and elegant system architecture with interpretable components: special control tokens provide transparent orchestration compared to opaque end-to-end models.
Comprehensive evaluation across 8+ diverse benchmarks (general multimodal, vision, temporal, mathematical, text recognition) and multiple model sizes.
Modular and extensible design that supports adding new expert models without retraining the orchestration layer.
Good latency reduction (10.3%) through parallel batch TTS processing with rigorous comparison of sequential vs parallel approaches.
weaknesses: Misleading 'training-free' framing: All expert models require extensive training. The actual contribution is 'no orchestration-specific training,' which is overstated in abstract and title.

Potentially unfair comparison with unified models: Orchestration inherently ensembles to best model per task, whereas GPT-4o/Qwen2.5-Omni aim for single unified architecture. Using 32B models for 60% of inference is computationally expensive but not emphasized.

Critical missing ablation studies: No isolation of contributions from controller routing vs. cross-modal memory vs. parallel TTS. No analysis of routing accuracy or how often controller correctly selects [S.need_vision], [S.need_reasoning], etc.

Heavy dependence on prompt engineering with reproducibility concerns: The critical 'dynamic prompt composer' is under-specified, only a basic template is shown in Appendix C, and no sensitivity analysis to prompt quality or controller LLM choice is provided.

Limited technical novelty: LLM-based routing via prompting is standard; JSON memory management is straightforward; parallel TTS is primarily engineering optimization. The combination is reasonable but incremental.

Insufficient error analysis: No evaluation of failure modes when controller makes incorrect routing decisions, no robustness testing across edge cases, no characterization of when orchestration helps vs. hurts.

Limited true multimodal evaluation: Most benchmarks are dominantly visual (MMBench, MMStar, Video-MME). Despite claiming focus on 'interactive multimodal interaction,' evaluation lacks user studies and relies on static benchmarks. Audio-visual integration is minimal.

Memory management under-evaluated: Content-aware compression strategy is proposed but not empirically validated. No comparison with alternative memory strategies or demonstration of long conversation handling.

Missing computational cost analysis: 3.2s response time includes multiple sequential model calls without detailed breakdown. Total computational requirements vs. unified models not thoroughly discussed.

Algorithm lacks important details: Algorithm 1 missing error handling for conflicting control tokens. Modality selection (Eq. 2) is trivial. TTS segmentation rules are rule-based and may not generalize across languages/domains.
No comparison with relevant baselines: Missing comparisons with simpler routing strategies (rule-based, learned routing without LLMs) or other LLM-based orchestration methods.

Reproducibility limitations: Some baseline results 'referenced from official papers' rather than reproduced. Prompt templates not fully shared. No code availability mentioned. Expert model versions not consistently specified.
